display.title: The Rebbe Maharash and Me'ayin Yavo Ezri: Help From Nowhere
display.summary_short: Falsely accused of cheating the Russian government, the Chassid Reb Shmuel Brin is told by the Rebbe Maharash to help any Jew who asks 'Where will my help come from?'
display.summary_long: Reb Shmuel Brin, a Chassid of the Rebbe Maharash, owns a busy vodka factory whose great tank is fitted with a government meter for taxes. A dishonest worker secretly drills a hole in the tank to steal drink, and a second worker joins him as a partner. When the two fall out and the police arrive, the thief blames his Jewish boss, and Reb Shmuel is arrested and faces Siberia. After a night of Tehillim and teshuvah he pours out his heart to the Rebbe Maharash, ending with the words 'Me'ayin yavo ezri', where will my help come from? The Rebbe explains that 'ayin' also means nothing: help can come from nowhere, and if a Jew in need ever says those words to him, he must fill that need completely. Back home, Reb Shmuel lends the whole sum to an innkeeper whose inn has burned down. At the trial the judge tells the jury how, as a stranded boy, he was fed and sent home by a kind stranger, the very man now accused, and the jury finds Reb Shmuel not guilty.
display.lesson: If you want Hashem to help you, help another Jew; kindness given without expecting anything back returns in unexpected ways.

advisories.note: Antisemitic police let a thief blame his Jewish employer, who is arrested and threatened with Siberia; he is acquitted.

characters: Reb Shmuel Brin, a Chassid of the Rebbe Maharash
